title: Hydration, fluid balance and IV fluids
blurb: Keep an accurate fluid balance, spot dehydration and overload, and apply NICE CG174 to IV fluid therapy and pumps.
question: Mr Kerr, 79, has heart failure and is receiving IV fluids overnight. At 03:00 he is breathless with a respiratory rate of 26, SpO2 92% on air and crackles at both lung bases. What should the nurse do first?

teach.body: Fluid balance is the difference between all fluid going into the body (oral, enteral, IV) and all fluid coming out (urine, vomit, drains, stoma, diarrhoea, nasogastric aspirate) over a set period, usually 24 hours. In plain English: a positive balance means more went in than came out; a negative balance means more came out. The chart is only useful if every input and output is measured and recorded at the time.

teach.h: The 5 Rs of IV fluid therapy
teach.caption: NICE CG174. Every IV fluid prescription should state which R it is for, and every patient on IV fluids is reassessed.

teach.caption: Plus 50–100 g/day glucose. Obese patients: use ideal body weight; rarely more than 3 L a day. For suspected sepsis follow NICE NG253 (250 mL boluses).

teach.body: New breathlessness, crackles and falling saturation during IV fluids in a man with heart failure point to fluid overload (pulmonary oedema). The nurse stops the infusion, sits him upright, gives oxygen to target, calculates NEWS2 and calls the doctor urgently using SBAR. She checks the fluid balance chart and the prescription: CG174 suggests 20–25 mL/kg/day for people with cardiac failure. She documents everything and reports it as a fluid mismanagement incident if appropriate.

Anyone continuing on IV fluids needs at least daily reassessment of clinical fluid status, urea, creatinine and electrolytes, and the fluid balance chart, plus weighing twice weekly. CG174 asks that clear fluid mismanagement (for example, prolonged dehydration or inadvertent overload) is reported as an incident so practice improves. CG174 also warns that adding potassium to IV fluid bags is dangerous: use ready-mixed bags.

children.label: Between pump and patient
children.sub: Clamps, kinks, three-way tap, cannula site

children.label: Between bag and pump

teach.caption: Never just silence and restart: find the cause, check the site, and record the volume actually given.

teach.text: A 'positive balance' is not automatically good, and a 'negative balance' is not automatically bad: a person with heart failure on diuretics may need to be negative. And older, frail people and those with heart or kidney failure need less maintenance fluid (20–25 mL/kg/day), not the standard 25–30.

items: Balance = total in minus total out; record every input and output at the time.
Hypovolaemia: SBP under 100, HR over 90, CRT over 2 s, RR over 20, NEWS2 5 or more (CG174 1.2.1).
Overload: breathless, crackles, oedema, falling SpO2: stop the fluids, sit up, escalate.
5 Rs; maintenance 25–30 mL/kg/day (20–25 if older, frail, cardiac or renal); 500 mL bolus under 15 min (sepsis: NG253).
Daily review of fluid status, U&E and chart; report fluid mismanagement as an incident.

summary: You can now calculate and interpret a fluid balance, distinguish dehydration from fluid overload, apply the NICE CG174 5 Rs and maintenance volumes, and troubleshoot an infusion pump alarm safely.

A.q: Mr Ellis, 70, has a 24-hour intake of 1,500 mL oral and 1,000 mL IV. His output is 1,600 mL urine and 400 mL vomit. What is his fluid balance?

whyNot.1: Output is less than intake, so the balance is positive.
whyNot.2: This leaves out the 400 mL of vomit.
whyNot.3: This leaves out part of the intake.

A.q: A newly registered nurse asks which list gives the NICE CG174 '5 Rs' of IV fluid therapy. Which is correct?
options: Rehydration, routine maintenance, replacement, redistribution, record-keeping
Resuscitation, routine maintenance, replacement, redistribution, reassessment
Resuscitation, routine maintenance, replacement, rate, reassessment
Resuscitation, rehydration, replacement, redistribution, regular review
A.why: NICE CG174: Resuscitation, Routine maintenance, Replacement, Redistribution and Reassessment.

whyNot.0: The first R is resuscitation, and record-keeping is not one of the 5 Rs.
whyNot.2: Rate is a prescription detail; redistribution is the missing R.
whyNot.3: Rehydration replaces routine maintenance, and the last R is reassessment.

A.q: Mrs Okeke, 86, lives in a care home and has had diarrhoea for 3 days, drinking very little. Which group of findings most suggests dehydration?
options: Bounding pulse, raised BP and ankle swelling
Crackles at the lung bases and breathlessness
Dry mouth, reduced urine output and tachycardia
Warm peripheries and a capillary refill of 1 second
A.why: Dry mucous membranes, low or concentrated urine and a raised heart rate are features of hypovolaemia (CG174 Table 1 and rec 1.2.1).

whyNot.0: These suggest fluid overload, not depletion.
whyNot.1: Crackles and breathlessness suggest pulmonary oedema.
whyNot.3: Warm peripheries and brisk refill suggest adequate perfusion.

B.q: Mr Shah, 55, weighs 70 kg and is nil by mouth after surgery. He has no cardiac, renal or nutritional problems. Using NICE CG174, what is an appropriate daily maintenance water volume?
B.why: Routine maintenance is 25–30 mL/kg/day: 70 × 25 = 1,750 mL and 70 × 30 = 2,100 mL.

whyNot.0: This is 15–20 mL/kg/day, below the CG174 range.
whyNot.1: This is 35–40 mL/kg/day, above the CG174 range.
whyNot.2: This is 20–25 mL/kg/day, the reduced range for frail or cardiac or renal patients.

B.q: Mrs Ford, 91, weighs 45 kg, is frail and has chronic kidney disease. Routine IV maintenance is prescribed at 30 mL/kg/day. What should the nurse do?
options: Query the prescription as a lower rate may be needed
Give it as prescribed, as 30 mL/kg/day is the standard
Double the rate for the first 6 hours to catch up
Change the fluid to glucose 5% without discussion
B.why: CG174 rec 1.4.3: consider 20–25 mL/kg/day for older or frail people and those with renal impairment. Raise it with the prescriber.

whyNot.1: 30 mL/kg/day is the upper end of standard maintenance, too high for her risk profile.
whyNot.2: Increasing the rate raises overload risk and is not prescribed.
whyNot.3: Changing a prescribed fluid without the prescriber is outside the nurse's authority.

B.q: Mr Long, 64, has IV fluids running through a volumetric pump. The pump alarms 'downstream occlusion'. What should the nurse check first?
options: The fluid bag, in case it is empty
The line, clamps and cannula site
The pump's battery and mains lead
The prescription for the correct rate
B.why: A downstream occlusion is between the pump and the patient: check for closed clamps, kinked tubing, a closed tap or a blocked or tissued cannula.

whyNot.0: An empty bag causes an upstream or air-in-line alarm.
whyNot.2: Power problems give a battery alarm, not an occlusion alarm.
whyNot.3: The prescription matters but does not cause an occlusion.

C.q: Mr Kerr, 79, has heart failure and is on IV fluids. At 03:00 he is breathless, RR 26, SpO2 92% on air, with crackles at both lung bases. What should the nurse do first?
options: Increase the rate to correct his low blood pressure
Encourage deep breaths and reassess in an hour
Stop the infusion, sit him up and escalate urgently
Record a fluid balance and hand over to the day team
C.why: Signs of pulmonary oedema during IV fluids (CG174 Table 1). Stop the fluids, sit him upright, give oxygen to target, calculate NEWS2 and escalate urgently.

whyNot.0: More fluid would worsen pulmonary oedema; his BP was not given as low.
whyNot.1: Waiting an hour delays treatment of a potentially life-threatening problem.
whyNot.3: This needs action now, not at handover.

C.q: Mrs Hart, 68, has been nil by mouth for 2 days with IV fluids only. Her urea has risen by 60% with no other cause, and her urine is dark and scanty. According to NICE CG174, how should this be handled?
options: Treat it and report it as a fluid mismanagement incident
Treat it and report it if she later develops kidney injury
Record it in the notes as an expected effect of surgery
Wait for the next routine blood test to confirm the trend
C.why: CG174 Table 1 lists hypovolaemia with features of dehydration, low or concentrated urine and over 50% rise in urea or creatinine as fluid mismanagement to report as a critical incident.

whyNot.1: CG174 asks for reporting of clear mismanagement without waiting for further harm.
whyNot.2: Calling it expected hides a preventable problem.
whyNot.3: She already has clinical and biochemical signs needing action.

C.q: Mr Diaz, 50, is hypotensive and tachycardic after a GI bleed. He does not have suspected sepsis. A crystalloid bolus is prescribed under NICE CG174. Which bolus fits CG174?
C.why: CG174: for fluid resuscitation give a 500 mL bolus of crystalloid containing sodium 130–154 mmol/L over less than 15 minutes, then reassess.

whyNot.0: 250 mL boluses are the NG253 approach for suspected sepsis.
whyNot.1: 1 litre over an hour is not the CG174 resuscitation bolus.
whyNot.2: 100 mL over 30 minutes is too small and too slow for resuscitation.

reteach.title: A bath with the tap and plug
reteach.question: Think of the body as a bath: the tap is intake and the plughole is output. What happens when one runs faster than the other?

blocks.body: If the tap runs faster than the plughole drains, the bath fills: positive balance. A heart or kidney that cannot cope is like a narrow plughole, so even a normal tap overflows (oedema, breathlessness). If the plughole is wide open (vomiting, diarrhoea, drains) and the tap is low, the bath empties: dehydration. Fluid balance charts measure the tap and the plughole; observations and weight tell you the water level.

How
rows: Measure every void or catheter bag

blocks.text: Unrecorded outputs (an unmeasured vomit, a wet pad not weighed) make a chart look falsely positive: record every loss.

explain.body: Add every input (oral, IV, enteral). Add every output (urine, vomit, drains, NG aspirate, stoma, diarrhoea). Subtract output from input. Positive = more in; negative = more out.

test.q: Intake 2,000 mL; output 2,400 mL. What is the balance?

whyNot.0: More went out than in, so it is negative.

explain.body: CG174 rec 1.2.1: systolic BP under 100, heart rate over 90, capillary refill over 2 seconds or cold peripheries, respiratory rate over 20, NEWS 5 or more, positive passive leg raise.

test.q: Which finding is a CG174 indicator for urgent fluid resuscitation?
test.why: CG174 rec 1.2.1 lists NEWS of 5 or more as an indicator for urgent fluid resuscitation.

whyNot.0: The threshold is a heart rate over 90.
whyNot.1: The threshold is systolic BP under 100.
whyNot.3: The threshold is capillary refill over 2 seconds.

explain.body: 25–30 mL/kg/day water; about 1 mmol/kg/day potassium, sodium and chloride; 50–100 g/day glucose. Consider 20–25 mL/kg/day for older or frail people, renal impairment, cardiac failure, malnutrition or refeeding risk.

test.q: For a frail 50 kg woman, what reduced maintenance range does CG174 suggest?

whyNot.1: This is 25–30 mL/kg/day, the standard range.
whyNot.2: This is 30–35 mL/kg/day, above both ranges.
whyNot.3: This is 15–20 mL/kg/day, below the reduced range.

explain.body: Overload: breathlessness, crackles, falling SpO2, oedema, rising weight: stop fluids, sit up, oxygen, escalate. Pump occlusion: downstream = clamps, kinks, taps, cannula; upstream = bag, roller clamp, line above the pump.

test.q: During IV fluids, Mrs Penn becomes breathless with new crackles. What is the first action?
test.why: Suspected fluid overload: stop the infusion first, sit her up and escalate urgently.

whyNot.2: Lying flat worsens breathlessness in pulmonary oedema.
whyNot.3: A diuretic needs a prescription and comes after stopping the cause and escalating.
